extracted.intended_audience: homeowners, farmers, sanitary engineers, and plumbers planning or constructing domestic water supplies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical standards for selecting, constructing, protecting, and operating domestic water supplies (wells, springs, brooks, ponds) including recommended construction details, pump options, storage and pressure considerations, and water-quality factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of water sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide possible sources of water for domestic consumption into two groups: those under the surface (wells and springs) and those on or above the surface (brooks, streams, lakes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to guide selection: wells are normal for households without plumbing; surface supplies are often required when large volumes are needed after installing modern plumbing, though quality may be questionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer well for basic household needs; surface supply for large-volume plumbing
rubrics_metrics.description: A well meets family requirements before plumbing; with modern plumbing a well may be pumped dry and a surface supply is often sought to secure an unfailing supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh convenience and quantity needs: choose wells for modest demand and surface supplies (with appropriate storage/filtration) when plumbing raises consumption significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shallow (dug) well construction dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary shallow/dug well: usually 10–20 feet deep; excavation about eight feet diameter with inside dimension about five feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dug by hand down to water using a boat pump to keep water down, then 'stoned up' with dry wall. Suitable for single-house supplies when water is near surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well wall cementing for pollution prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Wall should be well cemented beginning about six feet below the surface and reaching up to at least one foot above surface to prevent surface pollution access to the well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection greatly reduces risk from nearby cesspools/privies; illustrated contrast between protected and unprotected wells (Figs. 28–30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well curb/shoe design when sinking in sand
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a curb (several thicknesses of two-inch plank, joints broken in layers) supporting the lower course of masonry; have the shoe extend outward beyond the well walls to provide clearance so dirt will not hold the wall up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when sinking wells in water/sandy bottoms; requires a bucket that digs under water for full sinking—mainly practical for larger excavations with machinery but can be used for single-house wells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barrel/sewer-pipe sinking method in sandy bottom
rubrics_metrics.description: If bottom is sandy, sink a barrel or large sewer pipe into the bottom by removing material from inside and loading the outside to keep it pressed down; can be used to sink entire well wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique allows constructing a well in water/sand; requires suitable bucket for under-water digging; method is less customary for single-house work but feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of shallow wells from surface and subsurface contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Without cementing the wall to the recommended depth, surface wash and subsurface pollution may readily contaminate the water (illustrated in Fig. 28 vs. Fig. 29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a cesspool/privy is dangerously near, a properly cemented and covered well (with cover and wall extended) reduces danger to minimal terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Driven well methods and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Driven wells are often made by driving wrought-iron pipe into the ground, sometimes starting with 1.25-inch pipe driven in increments; suitable for soft ground or sand up to depths of about 100 feet and for testing ground water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Driven wells have no protection against pollution and are disadvantageous because the iron pipe may rust at the top of the ground water, admitting polluted drainage; they are most useful for testing and shallow uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-well drilling techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: For larger supplies and greater depths, use pile-driver-like machines to force down pipe, slip smaller pipes inside when limit reached, use drills inside last pipe to penetrate rock, and alternate drilling/pipe-driving/pumping or use water-jet methods to loosen and remove material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Churn and sand pump or water-jet methods (Fig. 32) are commonly used; sequence depends on soil/rock conditions and required depth—machinery and sand-pump or jetting are standard for deep installations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing yield by driving deeper or adding pipes
rubrics_metrics.description: If a dug well doesn't furnish required quantity, pipe wells may be driven to lower strata so water will rise into the dug well; sometimes driving further shuts off an earlier supply and reaches another layer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local conditions are uncertain—success in one well does not guarantee adjacent wells will be equally successful. Use cautious investment due to expense and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-well pump (inside-casing pump) suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a deep-well pump fitted inside the piping lowered to the water level when ordinary suction pumps cannot draw; ability to bring water depends on pump power and presence of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pump principle: submerged valve A and valve B on lower end of pump rod operate alternately to lift water at each stroke (illustrated in Fig. 22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-pressure (air-lift) method for deep wells
rubrics_metrics.description: Use compressed air delivered below the water level to cause water to rise either to the tank or to a point reachable by an ordinary pump; requires an air blower (engine) and is suited to occasional needs where engine is already available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple operation: air pipe delivers compressed air below water level; water rise distance depends on delivered air pressure (illustrated in Fig. 23). Not generally feasible where no engine exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring protection and enclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect spring from surface drainage by extending the surrounding wall above ground and making it impervious for at least six feet below the surface; consider converting an open spring into an underground one with a roof and sod cover (Fig. 33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ensure spring cannot be contaminated by surface drainage; enclosure and impervious walls are key protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending/gathering spring yield
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase yield by extending the spring outlet along the edge of the water-bearing stratum with stone-walled conduits covered with flat stones to form a pervious channel, or by digging a trench along the hillside and laying draintile surrounded by gravel or broken stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For single-house use, lay 3-inch terra-cotta tile in a short trench surrounded by gravel and cover over; trenches can collect multiple small springs or intercept underground flow (examples from Arkansas River Valley, South Platte near Denver).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting brook supplies: measure low-season flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding on a brook supply, measure volume at the time when it is lowest (probably about the middle of August) to ensure adequate flow for household needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very small flow (e.g., one quart in five minutes) can serve a family with storage, but small flows often require reservoirs to supply faucets at required rates and to avoid high temperatures promoting growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use storage/reservoirs to mitigate low-flow streams
rubrics_metrics.description: If brook flow is low or seasonal, provide a dam/pond or storage (cistern/barrel) to even out supply and improve quality by reducing temperature and biological growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger storage resists adverse effects of low flow and high temperature; even if stream dries for months, a suitable dam and pond may store water for domestic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ponds/lakes remote from habitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ponds in the midst of woods, far from human habitation, are excellent supplies; as country settles, ponds are likelier to become contaminated—factor this into planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pond water often contains vegetable decomposition coloring but may still be safe unless other pernicious pollutants are present; consider cooperative arrangements with neighbors to fence and dedicate small ponds for supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pond/reservoir water quality advantage: settling
rubrics_metrics.description: Water taken from a pond or reservoir is generally better than running water because contaminating substances tend to settle out; deep ponds/reservoirs usually yield better quality than the stream above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reservoirs reduce pollution risk compared to upstream stream conditions; use whenever feasible for improved quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended pressure/head for domestic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide about twenty feet of head above the highest fixture in the house whenever possible (more to offset frictional losses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This head ensures reasonable flow; frictional losses in long runs must be accounted for and additional head provided accordingly. Attic tanks producing only ~10 feet head may be slow but acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for friction losses; size pipe accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Frictional head loss in small pipes is appreciable and depends on pipe size and flow rate; use table of losses (e.g., loss in feet per 100 ft for various flow rates and pipe sizes) to select pipe diameter so available elevation difference suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for 7000 gallons/day over 4000 ft at 50 ft elevation difference, a 1-inch pipe would lose ~104 ft (insufficient) while a 1-1/4-inch pipe would lose ~39 ft and be acceptable. Too-small pipes can drastically reduce effective pressure (e.g., 1/2-inch pipe causing 47 ft loss per 100 ft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tower/tank placement must account for pipe-run friction
rubrics_metrics.description: When pumping to an elevated tank or building a tower, consider the vertical down, across, and up distances in the pipe run—these add to frictional loss requiring higher tank placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 50 ft pipe run with 1/2-inch pipe can lose ~23.5 ft; choose larger pipe (3/4-inch, 1-inch) to reduce necessary extra elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineral content tolerances and hardness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically, waters with total solids from 10 to 300 parts per million are acceptable; water with more than 100 grains per gallon of mineral salts is noticeably 'hard' and may be unsuitable for drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardness affects washing/soap use and sometimes perceived health effects; while some commissioners favored moderately hard water, no conclusive proof ties hardness to mortality. Consider taste, usability, and soap costs when choosing supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate soap loss/cost from hardness (Whipple formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soap loss for washing: about 2 ounces of soap per 100 gallons for each part of calcium carbonate per gallon (or Whipple's expression H/100 = D where H is hardness in ppm and D is cost in cents per 1000 gallons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Canisteo hardness 162.8 → costs ~1.6 cents per 1000 gallons in soap; Clifton Springs 208; Catskill 22.1. Use these to compare economic impact of hard well vs. soft surface supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness practical effects and cautions on health claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Within reasonable limits, little to choose between hard and soft water for drinking; claims linking hardness to diseases like calculus, cancer, goiter, cretinism are unproven; abrupt changes in hardness may cause temporary derangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider community experience and available evidence; prioritize other health-related contaminants over moderate hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small storage causes temperature rise and biological growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Very small storage for low-flow brooks raises summer water temperature so that vegetation and animal growths flourish, producing disagreeable taste and smell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid minimal storage; increase storage volume to reduce temperature rise and biological growth; larger quantity resists bad effects of low flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative arrangements for pond supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Neighbor cooperation—owner fences and dedicates pond, others pipe water—can make using a small pond economically feasible for several householders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider shared cost and mutual agreements when a pond is near multiple households; such collaboration mitigates individual expense and encourages pond protection.
